# A. What forecasting is for {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 1

## Forecasting drives decisions

::: {.incremental}
- **Inventory** — how much stock to hold
- **Staffing** — how many people to roster
- **Energy** — when generation must ramp up
- **Finance** — cash flow and budget targets
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .teal}
A forecast is only useful if it **changes a decision**.
:::

::: {.notes}
The decision dictates the entire setup: the forecast horizon, the time frequency, and the error metric you care about.
:::

## What can be forecast?

Three factors determine predictability:

::: {.incremental}
1. **Understanding** — how well we understand the drivers
2. **Data** — how much historical data exists
3. **Influence** — whether the forecast changes the outcome
:::

::: {.notes}
Point 3 is critical: if a demand forecast causes price cuts or stockouts, it alters future demand (self-fulfilling or self-defeating forecasts).
:::

## Predictability: Two extremes

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Electricity Demand]{.card-title}

- Clear drivers (weather, calendar)
- High volume of historical data
- Forecast does not change demand
- $\rightarrow$ **Highly predictable**
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[Exchange Rates]{.card-title}

- Weakly understood drivers
- Forecast moves the market
- No stable pattern
- $\rightarrow$ **Hard to beat today's price**
:::
:::
::::

## Three model types

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 9.5
digraph G {
    bgcolor="transparent";
    rankdir=LR;
    node [shape=box style="rounded,filled" fontname="Noto Sans" fontsize=13
          color="#1C355E" penwidth=2 margin="0.18,0.10"];
    edge [fontname="Noto Sans" fontsize=11 color="#5b6678" penwidth=1.6];

    E [label="1. Explanatory\nPredictors only\ny = f(weather, price, ...)"
       fillcolor="#00AE8D" fontcolor="white"];
    T [label="2. Time Series\nPast history of y only\ny(t) = f(y(t-1), y(t-2), ...)"
       fillcolor="#1C355E" fontcolor="white"];
    M [label="3. Mixed\nDrivers + history\ny(t) = f(drivers, y(t-1), ...)"
       fillcolor="#625D9C" fontcolor="white"];

    T -> M [label="add drivers"];
    E -> M [label="add history"];
}
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Course Focus
Days 1–2 focus on **pure time series** (Box 2). Day 3 covers mixed models.
:::

## Why past history often wins

Time series models only need to know: **what happened next last time?**

::: {.incremental}
- External drivers may not be available
- Future driver values are often unknown (e.g. future gas prices)
- The real system is often too complex to specify
:::

::: {.notes}
Relying on past history is not laziness; it is often the most robust, honest model choice in production.
:::

# B. What is in a time series {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

Ch 2 · Patterns and components

## Three core patterns

::: {.incremental}
- **Trend** — Long-term increase or decrease
- **Seasonality** — Repeating pattern at a **fixed, known period** (day, week, year)
- **Cycle** — Rises and falls with **no fixed period** (business cycles)
:::

::: {.notes}
Trend does not have to be linear. Cycles are usually longer than seasonality and vary in length.
:::

## Seasonality vs. Cycle

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Seasonality]{.card-title}

- **Known, fixed period**
- Driven by the calendar / clock
- Can be counted on reliably
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .navy}
[Cycle]{.card-title}

- **Variable, unknown period**
- Driven by economic / natural factors
- Turning points are hard to predict
:::
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## Common Mistake
Treating a cycle as seasonality causes models to predict peaks at the wrong time with false confidence.
:::

## Four series, four patterns

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 5.4))

P.plot_series(spine, ax=axes[0, 0], title="Trend + seasonality (retail)",
              ylabel="turnover ($M)")
P.plot_series(beer, ax=axes[0, 1], title="Seasonality + drifting trend (beer)",
              ylabel="megalitres")
P.plot_series(lynx, ax=axes[1, 0], title="Cycle, no fixed period (lynx)",
              color=P.ORANGE, ylabel="pelts traded")
P.plot_series(noise, ax=axes[1, 1], title="No pattern (white noise)",
              color=P.GREY, ylabel="z")
for ax in axes.ravel():
    ax.set_xlabel("")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The lynx peaks occur 8–11 years apart—never the exact same gap. This is a cycle, not seasonality.
:::

## Components of a time series

::: {.incremental}
- **Additive**: $y_t = S_t + T_t + R_t$
- **Multiplicative**: $y_t = S_t \times T_t \times R_t$
:::

. . .

| Component | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $S_t$ | **Seasonal** component (repeating calendar pattern) |
| $T_t$ | **Trend-Cycle** component (underlying direction) |
| $R_t$ | **Remainder** (random noise / unexplained variation) |

## Additive or Multiplicative?

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.9))
P.plot_series(beer.tail(120), ax=axes[0], color=P.BLUE, ylabel="megalitres",
              title="Additive: swing size is constant")
P.plot_series(souvenirs, ax=axes[1], color=P.ORANGE, ylabel="sales ($)",
              title="Multiplicative: swing grows with level")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cardbox .purple}
- Constant swing $\rightarrow$ **Additive**
- Growing swing $\rightarrow$ **Multiplicative** (fix with log transform)
:::

## The Golden Rule {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #625D9C)"}

::: {.r-fit-text}
The order **is** the data.
:::

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- Never shuffle time series data
- Never use random train/test splits
- Never use standard k-fold cross-validation
:::

::: {.notes}
Random shuffling allows models to look into the future. Day 2 introduces rolling-origin evaluation.
:::

## Shuffling destroys temporal signal

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
y = spine["y"].to_numpy()
shuffled = rng.permutation(y)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 5.2))
axes[0, 0].plot(spine["ds"], y, color=P.BLACK, lw=0.9)
axes[0, 0].set(title="Original data", ylabel="turnover ($M)")
axes[0, 1].plot(spine["ds"], shuffled, color=P.ORANGE, lw=0.9)
axes[0, 1].set(title="Shuffled (same values)", ylabel="turnover ($M)")
P.acf_plot(y, nlags=36, ax=axes[1, 0], highlight_every=12,
           title="Original ACF: Rich Structure")
P.acf_plot(shuffled, nlags=36, ax=axes[1, 1], color=P.ORANGE,
           title="Shuffled ACF: Zero Structure")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Mean and variance remain identical after shuffling, but every forecastable property is destroyed.
:::

# C. Seeing the patterns {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #9B8EC0)"}

Ch 2.2–2.5 · The essential plots

## Four diagnostic plots

| Plot | Core Question |
|---|---|
| **Time plot** | What does the overall series look like? |
| **Seasonal plot** | What is the repeating annual shape? |
| **Subseries plot** | How does each specific month/quarter evolve? |
| **Scatterplot** | Does another variable move in sync? |

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## Start with the Time Plot
Always check the time plot first for outliers, gaps, and structural breaks.
:::

## 1. Time plot

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.6))
P.plot_series(spine, ax=ax, ylabel="turnover ($M)",
              title=f"{D.SPINE_ID}, monthly")
plt.show()
```

::: {.incremental}
- Upward trend, roughly eightfold over 37 years
- The seasonal swing widens as the level rises
- A sharp step up in 2009 and a dip around 2000: ask what happened before modelling
:::

## 2. Seasonal plot

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
sp = D.add_calendar(spine)
recent = sp[sp["year"] >= sp["year"].max() - 9]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.7))
P.seasonal_plot(recent, "year", "month", ax=ax, season_labels=P.MONTH_LABELS,
                ylabel="turnover ($M)", xlabel="", colorbar=True,
                title="One line per year, last 10 years")
plt.show()
```

::: {.incremental}
- Every year peaks in **December** and troughs in **February**
- The shape repeats while the level climbs: that is seasonality, not cycle
:::

::: {.notes}
Ten years, not all 37. Over the full span the level grows eightfold, so the lines
stack by year and the shape is unreadable. Say that out loud, it is the same
problem the next slide makes explicit.
:::

## 3. Subseries plot: Seasonality isolated

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, axes = P.subseries_plot(D.add_calendar(beer), "quarter",
                             ylabel="megalitres", season_labels=P.QUARTER_LABELS,
                             title="Beer production by quarter (orange line = quarter mean)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cardbox .teal}
Differences in the horizontal means highlight the pure seasonal pattern.
:::

## 4. When trend swamps the subseries plot

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, axes = P.subseries_plot(sp, "month", ylabel="turnover ($M)",
                             season_labels=P.MONTH_LABELS,
                             title="Spine turnover by month, 1982 to 2018")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Trend Obscures Month-to-Month Means
When trend growth is massive (8x), seasonal differences appear tiny until trend is removed with **decomposition**.
:::

::: {.notes}
The seasonality is real (as seen in the seasonal plot), but raw monthly means fail to reveal it clearly under strong growth.
:::

## Always verify timestamps first

```{python}
#| echo: true
gaps = spine["ds"].diff().dt.days
print("Inferred frequency :", pd.infer_freq(spine["ds"]))
print("Duplicate stamps   :", spine["ds"].duplicated().sum())
print("Gaps > 1 month     :", int((gaps > 32).sum()))
```

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## Silent Gaps Break Models
A missing row shifts every seasonal lag that follows. Always check frequency before modelling.
:::

## Part 1 Recap {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #9B8EC0)"}

::: {.incremental}
- Forecasts exist to **inform decisions**
- **Trend, Seasonality, Cycle** are distinct patterns
- Multiplicative swings become additive under a **log transform**
- **Order is the data** — never shuffle
:::
